stages.name: Accept a connection and let the client speak first
hints: Bind a TCP listener on the port `-accept` names and accept in a loop; the port is chosen by the harness, never hardcoded
Say nothing on accept: TLS is client-speaks-first, and the ClientHello is the first byte either side sends
Set SO_REUSEADDR so a restart does not hit 'address already in use'
A client that connects and vanishes without a ClientHello is normal; close that socket and go back to accepting

tests.name: the server accepts a TCP connection
nothing is sent before the client speaks
a connection is accepted after an earlier one closed
ten connections in a row are all accepted
a client that disconnects without sending anything is survivable
two sockets can be open at once, and both get served
the server is still serving after all of that

stages.name: TLSPlaintext framing
hints: Every record is five header bytes — type(1), legacy_record_version(2), length(2) — and then exactly `length` fragment bytes
Read the five bytes first, then read `length` more; one read() is never one record, and one record is not always one message
legacy_record_version is 0x0303 everywhere, with one exception: the record carrying the first ClientHello may say 0x0301, and a server must accept it
The server's own records carry 0x0303; the real version is negotiated inside the ServerHello's supported_versions extension

tests.name: the ClientHello is answered when its record says 0x0303
the ClientHello is answered when its record says 0x0301
the server's first record is a handshake record
the server's first record carries legacy_record_version 0x0303
the server's records never exceed 2^14 fragment bytes
the record length agrees with the bytes that follow it
the ServerHello is a complete handshake message inside the record

stages.name: Record size limits
hints: TLSPlaintext.length may not exceed 2^14 (16384); a longer one is a record_overflow alert, not a bigger buffer
Check the length field before allocating: a two-byte length can ask for 65535 bytes that will never arrive
TLSCiphertext may be 2^14 + 256, which leaves room for the content type, the padding and the AEAD tag
A record that promises more bytes than the client ever sends must time out or close, never spin or wedge the accept loop

tests.name: a record claiming more than 2^14 fragment bytes is refused
a record exactly at the 2^14 limit is not refused for being too long
a length prefix that promises bytes the client never sends does not wedge the server
a zero-length handshake record is survivable
a record with length 0xffff is refused without allocating it
the server still serves a clean handshake after all of that

stages.name: Garbage on connect
hints: Validate the record's content type before anything else: a TLS 1.3 stream only ever starts with handshake(22)
A client that sends HTTP, SSH or noise gets an alert or a close — never a stack trace, never a hang, and never a dead accept loop
One bad connection must not take the others with it: handle each socket's errors where they happen
Whatever you decide, decide it quickly; a stranger must not be able to hold a connection open for ever by sending four bytes

tests.name: an HTTP request on the TLS port is refused
an SSH banner is refused
random bytes are refused
a record with an undefined content type is refused
a handshake record holding an unknown message type is refused
a single byte followed by silence is survivable
the server still serves a clean handshake afterwards

stages.name: A ClientHello split across segments and records
hints: TCP has no message boundaries: keep a buffer per connection and only act when a whole record is in it
A handshake message may span several records, so keep a second buffer for handshake bytes and only parse when msg_type's uint24 length is satisfied
Reassemble across records before parsing, never the other way round: the record boundaries are not part of the message
Only the handshake bytes go into the transcript — never the five-byte record headers, however the message was fragmented

tests.name: a ClientHello written one byte at a time is answered
a ClientHello split into two TCP writes is answered
a ClientHello split across three records is answered
a ClientHello whose first record holds only the header bytes is answered
the handshake completes normally after a fragmented hello
the transcript is over the message, not the records it arrived in

stages.name: Coalesced handshake messages
hints: One record may hold several handshake messages end to end; loop over the fragment until it is empty instead of parsing it once
The server's own flight is usually coalesced: EncryptedExtensions, Certificate, CertificateVerify and Finished often arrive in one or two records
Each message still gets its own four-byte header, and each goes into the transcript separately, in order
A record must never end in the middle of a message *and* start a new one — but a message may start in one record and finish in the next

tests.name: the server's encrypted flight is read whatever way it is packed
every message of the flight arrives exactly once
the flight's messages are in the order RFC 8446 fixes
a record carrying a ClientHello and trailing bytes is refused
the client's ChangeCipherSpec and Finished may be written together
the server's records are counted and reported

stages.name: Half-close and abandoned handshakes
hints: read() returning 0 is the peer's FIN: a normal end of stream, not an error and not a reason to abort the process
A client that shuts down its write half mid-handshake will never send more; drop that connection's state and carry on
Never let one abandoned handshake hold a resource for ever — the accept loop has to come back to accepting
A write to a socket the peer has closed is EPIPE or ECONNRESET; handle it where it happens rather than letting it end the process

tests.name: a client that half-closes before the ClientHello is survivable
a client that half-closes right after the ClientHello is survivable
a client that abandons the handshake mid-flight is survivable
a client that resets the connection after the ServerHello is survivable
ten abandoned handshakes in a row do not wedge the server
a clean handshake still works after every one of those

stages.name: legacy_version and supported_versions
hints: ClientHello.legacy_version is always 0x0303 and means nothing; never negotiate from it
The real version is in supported_versions(43): a one-byte-counted list in the ClientHello, a single uint16 in the ServerHello
ServerHello.legacy_version is 0x0303 too — a TLS 1.3 server puts 0x0304 in its own supported_versions extension and nowhere else
A ClientHello with no supported_versions extension is a pre-1.3 client; a 1.3-only server answers protocol_version(70)

tests.name: the ClientHello's legacy_version is 0x0303 and is ignored
the ServerHello's legacy_version is 0x0303
the ServerHello carries supported_versions with 0x0304
supported_versions in the ServerHello is exactly two bytes
a hello offering 1.3 among several versions still selects 1.3
an unrecognised legacy_version does not change the outcome
the negotiated version is 0x0304 and the handshake completes

stages.name: A TLS 1.2-only client is refused
hints: A hello with no supported_versions extension is a pre-1.3 client: a 1.3-only server answers protocol_version(70) and closes
A hello whose supported_versions list does not contain 0x0304 gets the same answer, however many other versions it lists
Send the alert as a plaintext record — there are no keys yet, and there never will be on this connection
The check comes before cipher-suite selection: the version decides whether the rest of the hello even means what you think it means

tests.name: a hello with no supported_versions extension is refused
a hello offering only TLS 1.2 is refused
a hello offering only TLS 1.0 and 1.1 is refused
the refusal is protocol_version(70) when an alert is sent
a hello offering 1.2 and 1.3 is accepted
the server still serves a 1.3 client afterwards

stages.name: Cipher-suite negotiation
hints: TLS 1.3 has three suites worth implementing: 0x1301 AES-128-GCM-SHA256, 0x1302 AES-256-GCM-SHA384, 0x1303 ChaCha20-Poly1305-SHA256
A suite names a hash *and* an AEAD; the hash drives the whole key schedule and the transcript, so picking 0x1302 means SHA-384 everywhere
The chosen suite must be one the ClientHello offered — a server that picks its own favourite regardless will fail every client's check
TLS 1.2 suite numbers may appear in the list; ignore them rather than choking on them

tests.name: TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256 alone is negotiated and works
TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384 alone is negotiated and works
TLS_CHACHA20_POLY1305_SHA256 alone is negotiated and works
the chosen suite is always one the client offered
a SHA-384 suite drives a SHA-384 key schedule
TLS 1.2 suite numbers in the list are ignored, not fatal
a duplicated suite in the list changes nothing
the suite is echoed in a single uint16, not a list

stages.name: No acceptable parameters: handshake_failure
hints: When no offered cipher suite is acceptable, the answer is a fatal handshake_failure(40) — not a ServerHello with a suite the client never offered
The same alert covers a client with no acceptable group and no acceptable signature algorithm
Send the alert in the clear: there are no handshake keys on a connection that never got past the hello
Close the connection after a fatal alert; there is no state left worth keeping

tests.name: a hello offering only TLS 1.2 suite numbers is refused
a hello offering an empty cipher suite list is refused
a hello offering only unknown suite numbers is refused
the refusal is a fatal alert, never a warning
a hello offering only an unimplementable group is refused
the server still serves an acceptable client afterwards

stages.name: key_share: x25519 and secp256r1
hints: The ClientHello's key_share carries a list of (group, key_exchange) pairs; the ServerHello's carries exactly one
x25519 key_exchange is 32 raw bytes; secp256r1 is a 65-byte uncompressed point starting with 0x04
The shared secret is the raw X coordinate — 32 bytes for both of these groups — and goes straight into HKDF-Extract as the IKM
Reject an all-zero x25519 result: it means the peer sent a small-order point (RFC 8446 section 7.4.2, RFC 7748 section 6.1)

tests.name: a hello sharing only x25519 completes
a hello sharing only secp256r1 completes
a hello sharing both groups gets exactly one back
the server's key_share names a group the client shared
an x25519 key_exchange is exactly 32 bytes
a secp256r1 key_exchange is a 65-byte uncompressed point
the shared secret is 32 bytes for both groups
the data path works under each group

stages.name: signature_algorithms and the server's key
hints: signature_algorithms(13) is mandatory in a TLS 1.3 ClientHello; a hello without it is missing_extension(109)
Pick a scheme the client offered *and* the server's own key can produce: an ECDSA P-256 key cannot sign rsa_pss_rsae_sha256
An RSA key in TLS 1.3 signs with RSA-PSS (0x0804/5/6), never PKCS#1 v1.5 — those code points exist only for certificate signatures
When nothing in the list fits the key, the answer is handshake_failure(40), not a signature the client cannot check

tests.name: an ECDSA key signs with ecdsa_secp256r1_sha256
an RSA key signs with RSA-PSS
an Ed25519 key signs with ed25519
the chosen scheme is always one the client offered
an ECDSA server refuses a client that only offers RSA-PSS
an RSA server refuses a client that only offers ECDSA
a hello with no signature_algorithms extension is refused
rsa_pkcs1_sha256 alone is not enough for an RSA key

stages.name: GREASE and unknown extensions are ignored
hints: An extension type you do not know is skipped, not an error: read its two-byte length and step over the body
The same goes for unknown cipher suites, groups, versions and signature schemes — skip the entry, keep reading the list
GREASE (RFC 8701) is the sixteen values 0x0a0a, 0x1a1a … 0xfafa; real clients send them deliberately to catch servers that do not skip
Never echo an extension back that the client did not send, and never send one in a ServerHello that RFC 8446 section 4.1.3 does not allow there

tests.name: a GREASE extension in the hello is ignored
several GREASE extensions at once are ignored
a GREASE cipher suite is ignored
a GREASE group and a GREASE key share are ignored
a GREASE version in supported_versions is ignored
an unknown extension carrying data is ignored
the ServerHello carries only extensions RFC 8446 allows there
the server never echoes an extension the client did not send

stages.name: SNI and ALPN
hints: server_name(0) is a list of (name_type, host_name) pairs; in practice it has exactly one entry of type host_name(0)
A server that accepted the name answers with an *empty* server_name extension in EncryptedExtensions, or with nothing at all — never with the name echoed back
ALPN lives in EncryptedExtensions too, and must name exactly one protocol, and that protocol must be one the client offered
A client that offers ALPN and a server that has no protocols configured is not an error: send no ALPN extension and carry on

tests.name: a hello with SNI completes
a hello with no SNI completes
SNI is never echoed with the host name in it
an unusual but legal host name is accepted
a hello offering ALPN completes either way
if ALPN is selected it is one the client offered
ALPN, if present in EncryptedExtensions, names exactly one protocol
a hello with neither SNI nor ALPN completes

stages.name: Session id echo, duplicate extensions, lying lengths
hints: legacy_session_id is echoed into the ServerHello byte for byte, whatever the client put there — 32 bytes, zero bytes, or anything between
A ClientHello with the same extension type twice is illegal_parameter(47); checking for it means keeping a set of the types you have seen
Every length must be checked against the bytes you actually have before you index; an extension claiming 400 bytes inside a 40-byte block is a decode_error
legacy_compression_methods must be exactly `01 00`; anything else is illegal_parameter

tests.name: a 32-byte legacy_session_id is echoed exactly
an empty legacy_session_id is echoed as empty
an odd-length legacy_session_id is echoed exactly
a duplicated extension is refused
an extension whose length runs past the block is refused
an extensions block whose length runs past the message is refused
a compression method other than null is refused
the server still serves a clean hello afterwards

stages.name: The ServerHello, field by field
hints: The body is legacy_version(2), random(32), legacy_session_id_echo(vec8), cipher_suite(2), legacy_compression_method(1), extensions(vec16) — in that order
random is 32 fresh random bytes; it is not a timestamp and not derived from anything the client sent
A TLS 1.3 server must not put the downgrade sentinels of RFC 8446 section 4.1.3 in the last eight bytes of random — those mean 'I negotiated 1.2 on purpose'
key_share and supported_versions are the two extensions that make this a TLS 1.3 ServerHello at all; everything else belongs in EncryptedExtensions

tests.name: legacy_version is 0x0303
legacy_compression_method is 0
random is 32 bytes and is not all zeros
random differs between two connections
random does not carry a TLS 1.2 downgrade sentinel
random is not the HelloRetryRequest value on a normal hello
key_share names a group and carries a share
the body ends exactly where its length says

stages.name: Early, Handshake and Master secrets
hints: Early Secret = HKDF-Extract(salt = Hash.length zeros, IKM = PSK or Hash.length zeros); with no PSK both inputs are zeros and the result is still not zero
Between Extract steps comes Derive-Secret(secret, "derived", "") — over the hash of the *empty* transcript, not the handshake so far
Handshake Secret = HKDF-Extract(salt = that derived value, IKM = the (EC)DHE shared secret); Master Secret = HKDF-Extract(salt = derived again, IKM = zeros)
HKDF-Expand-Label's info is uint16 length, then "tls13 " + label as an opaque<7..255>, then the context as an opaque<0..255> — the six-byte prefix includes the space

tests.name: the Early Secret is HKDF-Extract of two zero blocks
the Handshake Secret extracts the (EC)DHE secret under the derived salt
the Master Secret extracts zeros under the second derived salt
the handshake traffic secrets use the labels the RFC names
every derivation is over the hash length of the negotiated suite
getting the label wrong produces a different secret
the whole schedule is the one that decrypts the server's flight

stages.name: The transcript hash at every boundary
hints: The transcript is the concatenation of complete handshake messages — msg_type, the uint24 length and the body — and nothing else
Record headers, ChangeCipherSpec records and the AEAD's own bytes never enter it; a message that arrived in three records is hashed once
Keep a running hash context and take a snapshot at each boundary: four different hashes are needed at four different moments
The hash a signature or a MAC covers is the one *before* that message was added — CertificateVerify covers up to Certificate, Finished covers up to CertificateVerify

tests.name: the hash after the ClientHello is the hash of its bytes
the hash after the ServerHello covers both hellos
every boundary has a different hash
CertificateVerify signs the hash taken after Certificate
the server's Finished covers the hash before itself
ChangeCipherSpec records leave the transcript alone
the transcript is rebuilt from the messages and matches

stages.name: Traffic keys, IVs and the record nonce
hints: key = HKDF-Expand-Label(secret, "key", "", key_length) and iv = HKDF-Expand-Label(secret, "iv", "", 12); the context is empty for both
The nonce is the static IV with the 64-bit sequence number XORed into its right end — the number itself is never sent
The AEAD's additional data is the five bytes of the record header, exactly as written, with the *ciphertext* length in it
Every TLS 1.3 AEAD uses a 12-byte nonce and a 16-byte tag; only the key length changes between suites

tests.name: key and iv have the lengths the suite dictates
key and iv are HKDF-Expand-Label of the traffic secret
the nonce is the IV XOR the sequence number
the server's first encrypted record opens with the derived keys
the additional data is the record header with the ciphertext length
the client's and server's keys are different
every suite's keys open that suite's records

stages.name: The ChangeCipherSpec compatibility record
hints: TLS 1.3 has no ChangeCipherSpec message; the record survives only so the handshake looks like TLS 1.2 to a middlebox
Accept one (or several) at any point after the first ClientHello, ignore it, and keep the transcript and the sequence numbers untouched
It is always plaintext, even after keys are in force: content type 20, one fragment byte 0x01
Sending one is optional both ways; a client that sends none, and a client that sends three, must both get the same handshake

tests.name: a client that sends no CCS completes
a client that sends one CCS completes
a client that sends three CCS records completes
a CCS after the client's Finished is an unexpected record
the server's own CCS, if any, is plaintext and one byte
a CCS carrying a byte other than 0x01 does not crash the server
a CCS before the ClientHello does not crash the server

stages.name: EncryptedExtensions
hints: EncryptedExtensions is always the first message the server sends under the handshake traffic keys, and it is always sent — even when it is empty
Its body is one extensions block and nothing else: `08 00 00 02 00 00` is a perfectly good empty one
Only extensions that are *not* needed to establish keys go here: server_name, ALPN, max_fragment_length, and so on
key_share, pre_shared_key and supported_versions belong in the ServerHello; sending them here is unsupported_extension(110)

tests.name: EncryptedExtensions is sent on every handshake
it is the first message under the handshake keys
its body is exactly one extensions block
it never carries key_share, pre_shared_key or supported_versions
an empty EncryptedExtensions is six bytes long
it goes into the transcript like any other message
it arrives before Certificate, never after

stages.name: Record sequence numbers and key changes
hints: Each direction keeps a 64-bit counter of records written under the current keys; it is never sent, both sides just count
The counter resets to zero every time the keys change — handshake keys to application keys, and again after every KeyUpdate
ChangeCipherSpec records are not encrypted and do not advance either counter
A record that arrives out of order simply will not authenticate: the nonce is wrong, so the tag is wrong, and that is bad_record_mac

tests.name: the client's write counter is where it should be after the handshake
the counter resets when the handshake keys become application keys
many small records in a row all authenticate
the counter advances by one per record, not per byte
a ChangeCipherSpec record does not advance the counter
a record replayed at the wrong sequence number does not authenticate

stages.name: The Certificate message
hints: The body is certificate_request_context (an opaque<0..255>, always empty from a server) and then certificate_list, an opaque<0..2^24-1>
Each entry is cert_data (uint24-length DER) followed by its own extensions block — that per-entry block is new in TLS 1.3 and is usually two zero bytes
The end-entity certificate comes first, and each later entry should certify the one before it; the self-signed root may be left out
The certificate is sent encrypted, under the server handshake traffic keys, so it is not visible to a passive observer

tests.name: certificate_request_context is empty
the list holds at least one certificate
the first entry is a parsable X.509 certificate
the leaf's public key is the one that signed CertificateVerify
every entry carries its own extensions block
the message's lengths agree at all three levels
a three-certificate chain arrives leaf first
the Certificate message arrives encrypted, not in the clear

stages.name: CertificateVerify: context and transcript
hints: The signed content is 64 bytes of 0x20, then "TLS 1.3, server CertificateVerify", then a single 0x00, then Transcript-Hash(CH..Certificate)
The 64 spaces and the context string exist so a signature made here can never be replayed as a TLS 1.2 one, or as a client's
The body is algorithm (a uint16 SignatureScheme) and signature (an opaque<0..2^16-1>) — nothing else
Sign the transcript hash as it stood *before* this message; the message cannot cover itself

tests.name: the signature verifies over the documented content
it does not verify over the transcript hash alone
it does not verify under the client context string
it does not verify over the wrong transcript boundary
the 64 leading spaces are part of the signed content
the body is exactly algorithm and signature
the signature is fresh on every connection

stages.name: RSA-PSS, ECDSA and Ed25519 signatures
hints: rsa_pss_rsae_sha256 is RSA-PSS with MGF1-SHA-256 and a salt as long as the hash; the signature is exactly the modulus size
ecdsa_secp256r1_sha256 signs SHA-256 of the content and the signature is DER: a SEQUENCE of two INTEGERs, so 70-72 bytes and never fixed
Ed25519 is PureEdDSA: it signs the content itself, unhashed, and the signature is always 64 bytes
Whatever the scheme, the content is the same 64 spaces + context + 0x00 + transcript hash

tests.name: an ECDSA P-256 signature verifies and is DER-encoded
an RSA-PSS signature verifies and is 256 bytes
an Ed25519 signature verifies and is 64 bytes
the RSA signature is PSS, not PKCS#1 v1.5
the Ed25519 signature is over the content, not its hash
a one-bit change anywhere in the signature breaks it
the data path works under each key type

stages.name: The server's Finished
hints: finished_key = HKDF-Expand-Label(server_handshake_traffic_secret, "finished", "", Hash.length) — the context is empty
verify_data = HMAC(finished_key, Transcript-Hash(everything before this message))
The whole body is the verify_data: no length prefix, no algorithm field, just Hash.length bytes
Finished is the last message of the server's flight, and the transcript it covers is the one right after CertificateVerify

tests.name: verify_data is Hash.length bytes
verify_data is the HMAC the RFC describes
the finished key comes from the handshake traffic secret
a Finished computed with the client's key does not match
a Finished over the wrong transcript does not match
the body is the verify_data and nothing else
it works under every cipher suite

stages.name: The client's Finished, and what a wrong one costs
hints: The client's verify_data uses the *client* handshake traffic secret's finished key, over Transcript-Hash(everything up to and including the server's Finished)
It arrives encrypted under the client handshake keys, not the application keys — those only come into force once it has been sent
A wrong verify_data is decrypt_error(51), fatal, and the connection ends there
Only after this message is the handshake complete: application data written before it is early data, and that is a different feature

tests.name: a correct Finished is accepted
the client's verify_data uses the client's finished key
an all-zero verify_data is rejected with decrypt_error
a verify_data with one bit flipped is rejected
the server's own verify_data echoed back is rejected
a Finished of the wrong length is rejected
the server still serves a new connection after refusing one

stages.name: Wrong-order flights
hints: A TLS server is a state machine: decide what message is legal *next*, and refuse everything else with unexpected_message(10)
The client's whole first flight is one ClientHello; a second one is only ever legal as the answer to a HelloRetryRequest
Application data before the client's Finished is early data, and without an early_data extension there is nowhere for it to be decrypted
The check belongs before the parse: a message type that cannot occur here should never reach the code that decodes its body

tests.name: the server's own flight is in the order RFC 8446 fixes
a Finished sent instead of a ClientHello is refused
a second ClientHello with no HelloRetryRequest is refused
a KeyUpdate before the handshake completes is refused
a Certificate the server never asked for is refused
a ServerHello sent by the client is refused
application data before the client's Finished is refused
the server still serves a well-ordered handshake afterwards

stages.name: The -rev echo
hints: `-rev` is line-based: buffer bytes until a newline arrives, then answer that one line and keep the rest
Strip the trailing CR and LF, reverse the bytes that are left, and write them back followed by exactly one LF
An empty line — a lone newline — answers with a lone newline; there is nothing to reverse
Only complete lines are answered: a write with no newline in it gets nothing back until one arrives

tests.name: one line comes back reversed
the answer ends with exactly one newline
a CRLF line is answered with a bare LF
an empty line answers with an empty line
two lines in one write get two answers, in order
a line spread over two records is answered once
a write with no newline gets no answer until one arrives
a line of punctuation and digits round-trips byte for byte

stages.name: The data path under every suite
hints: The record layer does not care which AEAD it is using: same framing, same inner content type, same nonce rule
What does change is the key length (16 or 32 bytes) and, for the SHA-384 suite, every secret and transcript hash in the schedule
ChaCha20-Poly1305 has no block size, so its ciphertext is exactly the plaintext length plus the 16-byte tag — the same as GCM here
Test the data path under each suite separately: a key-schedule bug that only affects SHA-384 is invisible under the other two

tests.name: TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256 carries data
TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384 carries data
TLS_CHACHA20_POLY1305_SHA256 carries data
many lines in a row under every suite
the ciphertext is the plaintext plus one type byte and a 16-byte tag
every suite works over x25519
every suite works over secp256r1

stages.name: TLSInnerPlaintext and padding
hints: Inside an encrypted record the plaintext is `content || content_type || zeros`; the outer header always says application_data(23)
To find the real type, scan back from the end past every zero byte — the first non-zero byte is it
Any amount of zero padding is legal, including none, and a receiver must accept whatever it is sent without reading anything into it
A decrypted record that is entirely zeros has no content type at all: that is unexpected_message(10), not a record of type zero

tests.name: a record with no padding is accepted
a record with 16 bytes of padding is accepted
a record with 1000 bytes of padding is accepted
padding changes the record length but not the answer
the server's own records carry a valid inner content type
an all-zero decrypted record is refused
a record whose inner type is a type TLS does not define is refused

stages.name: Record sizes and volume
hints: A sender may split application data into records however it likes; a receiver must reassemble the stream and never assume one record is one message
Keep each protected record's length within 2^14 + 256; when the data is bigger, write several records
A megabyte of traffic is a few dozen records, not one: the size limit is on the record, not on the connection
Many tiny records are legal and expensive — 17 bytes of overhead each — but they must still all arrive, in order

tests.name: a record at the plaintext size limit is carried
a four-kilobyte line round-trips
a megabyte of lines round-trips
five hundred one-byte lines round-trip
a line split over many tiny records is answered once
every record the server sends is within the ciphertext limit
the connection still works after all of that

stages.name: close_notify in both directions
hints: close_notify is an alert record — level warning(1), description 0 — sent encrypted under the current application keys
It says 'I will write no more'; the other direction stays open until that side sends its own, which is why it is a warning and not fatal
A server that receives one should stop reading that connection and may answer with its own before closing the socket
A TCP close with no close_notify is a truncation: legal to tolerate, worth telling apart from a clean end of stream

tests.name: a close_notify from the client is accepted
the server answers with its own close_notify or closes
the alert is level warning(1), not fatal
the alert is encrypted, not sent in the clear
data written before close_notify still gets answered
a TCP close with no close_notify is survivable
the server still serves a new connection after a clean close

stages.name: A tampered record is bad_record_mac
hints: A record whose AEAD tag does not verify is bad_record_mac(20), fatal, and the connection is over — there is no retry and no resynchronisation
The additional data is the record header, so changing the length or the type byte breaks the tag just as surely as changing the ciphertext
Do not leak *why* it failed: a bad tag, a bad length and a bad type must all produce the same alert at the same moment
The alert goes out under the keys that are still in force; the connection is closed straight after it

tests.name: a flipped bit in the ciphertext is bad_record_mac
a flipped bit in the tag is bad_record_mac
a record whose header length was changed is bad_record_mac
a record replayed a second time is bad_record_mac
a record sealed with the wrong key is bad_record_mac
the connection is over afterwards, not merely unhappy
the server still serves a new connection

stages.name: The alert record
hints: An alert is a record of type 21 whose fragment is exactly two bytes: level, then description
In TLS 1.3 the level is decoration — every alert except close_notify and user_canceled is fatal whatever the byte says, and a fatal alert always closes the connection
Before keys exist alerts go out in the clear; afterwards they are encrypted like anything else, with an inner content type of 21
An alert record must never be split across records or coalesced with another: two bytes, one record

tests.name: an alert record is two bytes in a type-21 record
a pre-keys alert arrives in the clear
a post-handshake alert arrives encrypted
a fatal alert from the client closes the connection
a warning alert that is not close_notify does not hang the server
an alert record of the wrong length is refused
an unknown alert description is survivable
the server still serves a new connection afterwards

stages.name: Unknown and truncated handshake messages
hints: Check the uint24 length against the bytes you actually have before you index into the body
A handshake type you do not know is unexpected_message(10) — a server cannot skip it the way it skips an unknown extension, because it has no idea what state it would be in afterwards
A message whose body does not decode is decode_error(50); a message that decodes but is not legal here is illegal_parameter(47)
A truncated message is not an error until the connection ends: more bytes may still be coming, so wait, then fail cleanly

tests.name: a handshake type TLS does not define is refused
a message whose uint24 length is absurd is refused
a ClientHello truncated mid-body does not wedge the server
a ClientHello with trailing bytes after the extensions is refused
a zero-length handshake body is refused
a handshake message of type 0 (the TLS 1.2 HelloRequest) is refused
the server still serves a clean handshake afterwards

stages.name: Renegotiation is gone
hints: TLS 1.3 removed renegotiation: there is no HelloRequest, and a ClientHello after the handshake is unexpected_message(10)
Key rotation is KeyUpdate and nothing else; a peer asking for new keys is not asking to renegotiate anything
The renegotiation_info extension and the SCSV may still arrive from old clients — ignore them, do not act on them
Post-handshake authentication exists, but only when the client offered post_handshake_auth in its hello; without it a CertificateRequest is illegal

tests.name: a ClientHello after the handshake is refused
a HelloRequest after the handshake is refused
the server never sends a HelloRequest of its own
the renegotiation_info extension is ignored, not acted on
the renegotiation SCSV in the suite list is ignored
a CertificateRequest the client never allowed is refused
the server still serves a new connection afterwards

stages.name: Fifty connections at once
hints: Every connection needs its own state: keys, sequence numbers, transcript and read buffer. Anything shared between them is a bug waiting for load
A server may serve connections one at a time or in parallel; both are conformant, and both must finish all fifty
Never let one slow or stuck client stop the accept loop — a listen backlog is not a queue you can ignore
Close each connection's socket when it ends rather than when the process does, or a long-lived server runs out of file descriptors

tests.name: fifty connections opened at once all complete
each connection gets its own answer, never another's
fifty sequential connections all complete
connections that are opened and abandoned do not block the others
two hundred connect-and-close cycles leak nothing
the server still serves a clean handshake afterwards

stages.name: Fuzz: four hundred mutated hellos
hints: Validate every length against the bytes you actually have before you index — that one rule survives most of this stage
A malformed input is at worst a closed connection: never a panic, never an unbounded allocation, never a loop that does not end
The accept loop has to outlive every bad connection; test that by sending a clean handshake afterwards, which is what this stage does
Everything here comes from --seed, so a failure is reproducible: the report names the round and the mutation that broke it

tests.name: four hundred mutated ClientHellos leave the server standing
every mutation kind is survivable on its own
a hundred records of pure noise are survivable
mutations after a completed handshake are survivable
the same seed produces the same corpus
a clean handshake still works after all of it

stages.name: HelloRetryRequest
hints: A HelloRetryRequest *is* a ServerHello: same message type, same fields, and a random fixed at SHA-256("HelloRetryRequest")
Its key_share carries only a selected_group and no share; the client answers with a second ClientHello carrying a share for that group
Before the retry goes into the transcript, ClientHello1 is replaced by the synthetic `message_hash` message of RFC 8446 section 4.4.1 — this is the one rule nobody guesses
A cookie, if one is sent, must be echoed back verbatim in the second hello and nowhere else

tests.name: a hello with no key share earns a HelloRetryRequest
the retry's random is SHA-256 of "HelloRetryRequest"
the retry names a group the client offered
the retry carries supported_versions and a key_share of two bytes
the handshake completes after the retry
the transcript uses the synthetic message_hash message
a cookie, if one is sent, is echoed in the second hello
data flows on a connection that began with a retry

stages.name: KeyUpdate
hints: The body is one byte: update_not_requested(0) or update_requested(1)
The new secret is HKDF-Expand-Label(old secret, "traffic upd", "", Hash.length); key and iv are expanded from it exactly as before
Only the sender's own direction changes, and the sequence number goes back to zero; the KeyUpdate itself is the last record under the old keys
update_requested(1) obliges the peer to send its own KeyUpdate back — and that answer must say update_not_requested, or two peers would ping-pong for ever

tests.name: data keeps flowing after update_not_requested
update_requested earns a KeyUpdate back
the write keys really change
the sequence number resets on the updated direction
several updates in a row all work
a KeyUpdate with an undefined request_update is refused
a KeyUpdate with a body of the wrong length is refused

stages.name: NewSessionTicket and resumption
hints: A ticket's PSK is HKDF-Expand-Label(resumption_master_secret, "resumption", ticket_nonce, Hash.length) — the nonce is what makes two tickets from one connection different
pre_shared_key must be the *last* extension of the ClientHello, because the binder is computed over everything before it
binder = HMAC(finished_key(binder_key), Transcript-Hash(truncated ClientHello)), where the truncation stops just before the binder list's own length
A resumed handshake sends no Certificate and no CertificateVerify: the PSK is the authentication

tests.name: the server sends a NewSessionTicket
the ticket's fields are well-formed
two tickets from one connection have different nonces
a ticket resumes the session
a resumed handshake sends no Certificate
data flows on a resumed connection
a wrong binder does not resume
an unknown ticket falls back to a full handshake

stages.name: Early data, offered and refused
hints: Early data is only on offer when the *ticket* said so: a NewSessionTicket with no early_data extension means 0-RTT is not available on it
A client may send early_data in its hello anyway; a server that does not want it simply leaves early_data out of EncryptedExtensions
When early data is refused there is no EndOfEarlyData message — that only exists on a connection where the server accepted it
Refusing is always safe and often right: 0-RTT data is replayable, and RFC 8446 appendix E.5 spends several pages on why

tests.name: a ticket without early_data does not permit 0-RTT
offering early_data anyway still completes the handshake
the server does not accept early data it never advertised
EncryptedExtensions carries no early_data extension
no EndOfEarlyData is expected on a refused connection
data flows normally after early data was refused
offering early_data without a PSK is ignored

stages.name: Real-client interop
hints: The suite's own client is one implementation; a second, independent one is the only way to find the places where both of yours agree and the RFC does not
`openssl s_client -tls1_3 -connect host:port` is the shortest full TLS 1.3 client there is, and it prints the negotiated parameters
Its `-ciphersuites` and `-groups` flags pin the negotiation, so each of the three suites and both groups can be exercised from the outside
`-sess_out` then `-sess_in` proves resumption end to end: the second run prints `Reused` when the ticket was accepted

tests.name: openssl s_client completes a handshake
openssl s_client gets its line reversed
openssl s_client reports TLSv1.3
openssl s_client negotiates each of the three suites
openssl s_client negotiates over secp256r1 as well as x25519
openssl s_client verifies the certificate against its own CA file
openssl s_client resumes with a ticket
curl over this contract is not a meaningful test
the suite's own client still works after all of that

stages.name: CertificateRequest
hints: CertificateRequest is handshake type 13 and belongs in the encrypted flight, after EncryptedExtensions and before the server's own Certificate

Its body is certificate_request_context (opaque<0..255>, empty during a handshake) followed by an extensions block — there is no certificate_types or supported_signature_algorithms list any more, those were TLS 1.2
signature_algorithms is mandatory in it: without it the client has no way to know what it may sign with, so an empty extensions block is an illegal message
Sending it at all is a choice; a server that never wants client certificates simply omits the message and nothing else about the handshake changes

tests.name: the server sends one when it is asking
it arrives inside the encrypted flight
it comes before the server's own Certificate
the context is empty during a handshake
it carries signature_algorithms
the schemes it offers are ones a TLS 1.3 client can use
requiring a certificate looks the same on the wire as requesting one
a server that was not asked for client auth sends none

stages.name: The client's Certificate and CertificateVerify
hints: Both messages go out under the *client* handshake traffic keys, after the server's Finished and before the client's own
The client's Certificate echoes the certificate_request_context byte for byte — empty during a handshake, but echoing is the rule

CertificateVerify signs 64 spaces, then "TLS 1.3, client CertificateVerify", then a zero byte, then the transcript hash up to and including the client's Certificate — a different context string from the server's, on purpose
The client's Certificate and CertificateVerify are in the transcript, so the Finished that follows covers them and its verify_data differs from an unauthenticated handshake's

tests.name: a client certificate completes the handshake
and the data path still works afterwards
the client's Certificate echoes the request context
the CertificateVerify uses a scheme the server offered
the client's messages are in the transcript before its Finished
a signature over the server's context string is refused
a signature over the wrong transcript is refused
a certificate the server's CA never signed is refused

stages.name: Declining, and requesting against requiring
hints: Declining is an empty Certificate, not silence: the client still sends the message, with a zero-length certificate_list, and no CertificateVerify after it
A server that only *requests* must carry on with an unauthenticated connection — the handshake completes and application data flows
A server that *requires* must fail the handshake, and certificate_required(116) is the alert that says why; handshake_failure loses that information
An empty Certificate is followed by Finished and nothing else — a CertificateVerify with no certificate to verify is an illegal message

tests.name: a client that declines sends an empty Certificate, not silence
a server that only requests carries on without one
and its data path works unauthenticated
a server that requires one refuses the empty list
and says certificate_required rather than something vaguer
authenticating against the same server succeeds
